#!/usr/bin/env python
# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-

import scrapy
import logging
from jobboard_scraper.items import JobItem, CompanyItem

class JobBoardSpider(scrapy.Spider):
    name = 'job_board'
    allowed_domains = ['example-jobboard.com']
    # Start URL(s) for job listing pages
    start_urls = ['https://www.example-jobboard.com/jobs']

    custom_settings = {
        'ROBOTSTXT_OBEY': True,  # Respect robots.txt
        'LOG_LEVEL': 'INFO',    # Set log level
        # Enable pipelines if needed:
        # 'ITEM_PIPELINES': { 'jobboard_scraper.pipelines.JsonWriterPipeline': 300, },
        # Feed export settings (for JSON output; change extension to .csv to get CSV output)
        'FEEDS': {
            'jobs_output.json': {
                'format': 'json',
                'encoding': 'utf8',
                'store_empty': False,
                'indent': 4,
            },
            'companies_output.json': {
                'format': 'json',
                'encoding': 'utf8',
                'store_empty': False,
                'indent': 4,
            }
        }
    }

    def parse(self, response):
        """
        Parse the job listings page.
        """
        self.logger.info("Parsing job listing page: %s", response.url)

        # Extract job posting links from the listing page.
        job_posting_links = response.css("div.job-posting a.job-link::attr(href)").getall()
        for relative_url in job_posting_links:
            url = response.urljoin(relative_url)
            yield scrapy.Request(url, callback=self.parse_job, errback=self.errback_handler)

        # Pagination handling: Assuming there's a link with rel="next"
        next_page = response.css("a[rel=next]::attr(href)").get()
        if next_page:
            next_page_url = response.urljoin(next_page)
            self.logger.info("Following pagination link to: %s", next_page_url)
            yield scrapy.Request(next_page_url, callback=self.parse, errback=self.errback_handler)
        else:
            self.logger.info("No further pagination links found.")

    def parse_job(self, response):
        """
        Parse individual job posting page.
        """
        self.logger.info("Parsing job posting: %s", response.url)
        job_item = JobItem()

        try:
            job_item['job_id'] = response.css("div.job-id::text").get(default="").strip()
            job_item['job_title'] = response.css("h1.title::text").get(default="").strip()
            job_item['company_name'] = response.css("a.company::text").get(default="").strip()
            job_item['is_remote'] = response.css("span.remote::text").get(default="false").strip() == "Remote"
            job_item['paid_relocation'] = 'yes' in response.css("span.relocation::text").get(default="").lower()
            job_item['visa_sponsorship'] = 'yes' in response.css("span.visa-sponsorship::text").get(default="").lower()
            job_item['onsite_limited_remote'] = 'limited remote' in response.css("span.onsite::text").get(default="").lower()
            job_item['high_response_rate'] = 'high' in response.css("span.response-rate::text").get(default="").lower()
            job_item['time_posted'] = response.css("time.posted::attr(datetime)").get()
            job_item['likes'] = int(response.css("span.likes::text").get(default="0"))
            job_item['dislikes'] = int(response.css("span.dislikes::text").get(default="0"))
            job_item['love_reactions'] = int(response.css("span.love::text").get(default="0"))
            job_item['salary_range'] = response.css("div.salary-range::text").get(default="").strip()
            job_item['equity_options'] = response.css("div.equity::text").get(default="").strip()
            job_item['required_experience'] = response.css("div.experience::text").get(default="").strip()
            job_item['job_type'] = response.css("div.job-type::text").get(default="").strip()
            job_item['role'] = response.css("div.role::text").get(default="").strip()
            job_item['industries'] = response.css("div.industries::text").getall()  # list of strings
            job_item['technologies_required'] = response.css("div.technologies::text").getall()  # list of strings
            job_item['full_description'] = response.css("div.full-description").get()
            job_item['employer_note'] = response.css("div.employer-note::text").get(default="").strip()
            job_item['preferred_timezone'] = response.css("div.preferred-timezone::text").get(default="").strip()
            job_item['office_location'] = response.css("div.office-location::text").get(default="").strip()
            job_item['visa_details'] = response.css("div.visa-details::text").get(default="").strip()
            job_item['relocation_details'] = response.css("div.relocation-details::text").get(default="").strip()
            job_item['source_control'] = response.css("div.source-control::text").get(default="").strip()
            job_item['one_step_build_supported'] = response.css("div.one-step-build::text").get(default="").strip().lower() in ['yes', 'true']
            job_item['daily_build_frequency'] = response.css("div.daily-build::text").get(default="").strip()
            job_item['uses_bug_database'] = response.css("div.bug-database::text").get(default="").strip().lower() in ['yes', 'true']
            job_item['bugfix_policy'] = response.css("div.bugfix-policy::text").get(default="").strip()
            job_item['schedule_uptodate'] = response.css("div.schedule::text").get(default="").strip().lower() in ['yes', 'true']
            job_item['specs_available'] = response.css("div.specs::text").get(default="").strip().lower() in ['yes', 'true']
            job_item['quiet_working_conditions'] = response.css("div.quiet::text").get(default="").strip().lower() in ['yes', 'true']
            job_item['best_tools_provided'] = response.css("div.best-tools::text").get(default="").strip().lower() in ['yes', 'true']
            job_item['dedicated_testers'] = response.css("div.testers::text").get(default="").strip().lower() in ['yes', 'true']
            job_item['code_screening'] = response.css("div.code-screening::text").get(default="").strip().lower() in ['yes', 'true']
            job_item['hallway_testing'] = response.css("div.hallway-testing::text").get(default="").strip().lower() in ['yes', 'true']
        except Exception as e:
            self.logger.error("Error parsing job posting (%s): %s", response.url, e)

        # Yield the job item
        yield job_item

        # Follow the company detail link from the job page if present
        company_detail_url = response.css("a.company-info::attr(href)").get()
        if company_detail_url:
            yield scrapy.Request(response.urljoin(company_detail_url),
                                 callback=self.parse_company,
                                 errback=self.errback_handler,
                                 meta={'company_name': job_item.get('company_name')})

    def parse_company(self, response):
        """
        Parse each company's detailed page.
        """
        self.logger.info("Parsing company page: %s", response.url)
        company_item = CompanyItem()

        try:
            company_item['company_name'] = response.meta.get('company_name') or response.css("h1.company-name::text").get(default="").strip()
            company_item['company_size'] = response.css("div.company-size::text").get(default="").strip()
            company_item['current_status'] = response.css("div.status::text").get(default="").strip()
            company_item['industry'] = response.css("div.industry::text").get(default="").strip()
            company_item['year_founded'] = response.css("div.founded::text").get(default="").strip()
            company_item['locations'] = response.css("div.locations span::text").getall()  # list of locations
            company_item['technologies_used'] = response.css("div.technologies-used span::text").getall()
            company_item['about'] = response.css("div.about").get(default="").strip()
            company_item['benefits'] = response.css("div.benefits li::text").getall()  # list of benefits
            company_item['key_people'] = response.css("div.key-people li::text").getall()
            company_item['current_job_openings'] = response.css("div.openings li::text").getall()
        except Exception as e:
            self.logger.error("Error parsing company (%s): %s", response.url, e)

        yield company_item

    def errback_handler(self, failure):
        """
        Log all failures.
        """
        self.logger.error(repr(failure))
        if failure.check(scrapy.spidermiddlewares.httperror.HttpError):
            response = failure.value.response
            self.logger.error("HTTP Error on %s", response.url)
        elif failure.check(scrapy.downloadermiddlewares.httpproxy.HttpProxyError):
            self.logger.error("Proxy Error on %s", failure.request.url)
        elif failure.check(scrapy.exceptions.IgnoreRequest):
            self.logger.error("IgnoreRequest on %s", failure.request.url)
        # More error checks can be added here as needed.

Write a Python function `calculate_bandwidth_overhead` that computes the bandwidth overhead introduced by a perturbation technique on network traffic data. The function should take two file paths as input: one for the original network traffic data and one for the perturbed network traffic data. Both files are in CSV format and contain network traffic data, where each row represents a sequence of packet sizes.

The function should use a utility function `load_csv_data` from a module `utils_wf` to load the data from the CSV files. The `load_csv_data` function returns two items: a list of packet size sequences (x) and their corresponding labels (y).

The bandwidth overhead is calculated as the absolute difference in the sum of absolute packet sizes between the original and perturbed data, divided by the sum of absolute packet sizes of the original data.

The function should return the bandwidth overhead as a float.
code:
```python
import numpy as np
from some_module import utils_wf  # Assuming utils_wf is in some_module

def calculate_bandwidth_overhead(original_path, perturbed_path):
    """
    Calculate the bandwidth overhead introduced by a perturbation technique on network traffic data.
    
    Parameters:
    original_path (str): The file path to the CSV containing the original network traffic data.
    perturbed_path (str): The file path to the CSV containing the perturbed network traffic data.
    
    Returns:
    float: The calculated bandwidth overhead.
    """
    # Load the original and perturbed data using the utility function
    x1, y1 = utils_wf.load_csv_data(original_path)
    x2, y2 = utils_wf.load_csv_data(perturbed_path)
    
    # Calculate the sum of absolute packet sizes for original and perturbed data
    ori = np.sum(np.abs(np.array(x1)))
    pertb = np.sum(np.abs(np.array(x2)))
    
    # Calculate the noise introduced by the perturbation
    noise = np.abs(pertb - ori)
    
    # Calculate the bandwidth overhead
    bandwidth_overhead = noise / ori
    
    return bandwidth_overhead

# Test cases to verify the solution correctness
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Assuming the paths to the CSV files are correct and utils_wf is properly implemented
    original_path = '../data/NoDef/ow/train_NoDef_sampled.csv'
    perturbed_path = '../data/WalkieTalkie/ow/adv_train_WalkieTalkie.csv'
    
    overhead = calculate_bandwidth_overhead(original_path, perturbed_path)
    print(f'Bandwidth overhead: {overhead}')
```

Below is one complete Python implementation that meets your specifications. In this solution the function uses os.path.exists to check for file existence, loads the CSV data via the utility function load_csv_data from the module utils_wf, verifies that every packet size is numeric, and then computes the bandwidth overhead as the absolute difference between the total absolute packet sizes (original versus perturbed) divided by the original total. Unit tests are also provided using the unittest framework along with monkey‐patching of os.path.exists and load_csv_data to simulate different scenarios.

# BEGIN CODE

#!/usr/bin/env python3

import os
from utils_wf import load_csv_data  # utility function: returns (x, y) where x is a list of packet sequences

def calculate_bandwidth_overhead(original_file_path, perturbed_file_path):
    """
    Compute the bandwidth overhead introduced by a perturbation technique.

    The overhead is defined as:
         overhead = |sum(|original|) - sum(|perturbed|)| / sum(|original|)
    
    Both CSV files are loaded with load_csv_data (which returns a tuple of (x, y)),
    and each packet size is expected to be numeric (int or float). Non-numeric
    values will result in a ValueError. If the original file's sum is zero a ValueError is raised.

    Parameters:
       original_file_path (str): Path to the original network traffic CSV file.
       perturbed_file_path (str): Path to the perturbed network traffic CSV file.

    Returns:
       float: The calculated overhead.

    Raises:
       FileNotFoundError: If either file path does not exist.
       ValueError: If any packet size cannot be converted to a float or if the original total is zero.
    """
    # Check that both files exist.
    if not os.path.exists(original_file_path):
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"Original file not found: {original_file_path}")
    if not os.path.exists(perturbed_file_path):
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"Perturbed file not found: {perturbed_file_path}")

    # Load the CSV data using the provided utility function.
    original_x, _ = load_csv_data(original_file_path)
    perturbed_x, _ = load_csv_data(perturbed_file_path)

    # To handle large files, processing may be done in chunks if load_csv_data supports it.
    # Here, we iterate over the sequences without accumulating the entire dataset in a new structure.
    
    def compute_total_abs(packet_sequences, label):
        total = 0.0
        for sequence in packet_sequences:
            for pkt in sequence:
                try:
                    # Convert or check that pkt is numeric.
                    pkt_value = float(pkt)
                except (ValueError, TypeError):
                    raise ValueError(f"Non-numeric packet size encountered in {label} data: {pkt}")
                total += abs(pkt_value)
        return total

    original_total = compute_total_abs(original_x, "original")
    perturbed_total = compute_total_abs(perturbed_x, "perturbed")

    if original_total == 0:
        raise ValueError("Sum of absolute original packet sizes is zero, cannot compute overhead.")

    overhead = abs(original_total - perturbed_total) / original_total
    return overhead


# Unit tests for the calculate_bandwidth_overhead function.
import unittest
from unittest.mock import patch

class TestCalculateBandwidthOverhead(unittest.TestCase):

    @patch('os.path.exists', return_value=True)
    @patch('utils_wf.load_csv_data')
    def test_valid_overhead_calculation(self, mock_load_csv_data, mock_exists):
        # Test with valid numeric data.
        # Original data: two sequences: [100, -50] and [200, -150]
        # Perturbed data: [90, -45] and [210, -140]
        # Expected:
        #   sum(original) = 100 + 50 + 200 + 150 = 500
        #   sum(perturbed) = 90 + 45 + 210 + 140 = 485
        #   overhead = abs(500 - 485) / 500 = 15/500 = 0.03
        original_data = ([[100, -50], [200, -150]], ["label1", "label2"])
        perturbed_data = ([[90, -45], [210, -140]], ["label1", "label2"])

        # Define a side effect function: decide which data to return based on the file path.
        def side_effect(file_path):
            if "original" in file_path:
                return original_data
            else:
                return perturbed_data

        mock_load_csv_data.side_effect = side_effect

        overhead = calculate_bandwidth_overhead("original.csv", "perturbed.csv")
        self.assertAlmostEqual(overhead, 0.03, places=5)

    @patch('os.path.exists', side_effect=lambda path: False if "missing" in path else True)
    def test_file_not_found(self, mock_exists):
        # If either file is missing, the function should raise a FileNotFoundError.
        with self.assertRaises(FileNotFoundError):
            calculate_bandwidth_overhead("missing_original.csv", "perturbed.csv")
        with self.assertRaises(FileNotFoundError):
            calculate_bandwidth_overhead("original.csv", "missing_perturbed.csv")

    @patch('os.path.exists', return_value=True)
    @patch('utils_wf.load_csv_data')
    def test_non_numeric_data_in_original(self, mock_load_csv_data, mock_exists):
        # Test when original data contains a non-numeric value.
        original_data = ([["100", "non_numeric"], [200]], ["l1", "l2"])
        perturbed_data = ([[90, -45], [210]], ["l1", "l2"])

        def side_effect(file_path):
            if "original" in file_path:
                return original_data
            else:
                return perturbed_data

        mock_load_csv_data.side_effect = side_effect

        with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
            calculate_bandwidth_overhead("original.csv", "perturbed.csv")

    @patch('os.path.exists', return_value=True)
    @patch('utils_wf.load_csv_data')
    def test_non_numeric_data_in_perturbed(self, mock_load_csv_data, mock_exists):
        # Test when perturbed data contains a non-numeric value.
        original_data = ([[100, -50], [200, -150]], ["l1", "l2"])
        perturbed_data = ([["90", "-45"], ["non_numeric", 140]], ["l1", "l2"])

        def side_effect(file_path):
            if "original" in file_path:
                return original_data
            else:
                return perturbed_data

        mock_load_csv_data.side_effect = side_effect

        with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
            calculate_bandwidth_overhead("original.csv", "perturbed.csv")

    @patch('os.path.exists', return_value=True)
    @patch('utils_wf.load_csv_data')
    def test_original_total_zero(self, mock_load_csv_data, mock_exists):
        # Test when the original data has a total of zero (all packet sizes are 0).
        original_data =  ([[0, 0], [0]], ["l1", "l2"])
        perturbed_data =  ([[0, 0], [0]], ["l1", "l2"])

        def side_effect(file_path):
            if "original" in file_path:
                return original_data
            else:
                return perturbed_data

        mock_load_csv_data.side_effect = side_effect
        with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
            calculate_bandwidth_overhead("original.csv", "perturbed.csv")

if __name__ == '__main__':
    unittest.main()

6. Classify a single image or a batch of images and print the predicted category indices.
7. Provide a command-line interface to classify images specified by the user.

```python
import os
import sys
import tensorflow as tf
import numpy as np

# Assuming resize_data and batch_maker are available and provide the necessary functionality
import resize_data
import batch_maker

BASE_DIR = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))

n_classes = 10
keep_rate = 0.7

weights = {
    'W_conv1': tf.Variable(tf.random_normal([5, 5, 1, 32])),
    'W_conv2': tf.Variable(tf.random_normal([5, 5, 32, 64])),
    'W_fc': tf.Variable(tf.random_normal([8 * 8 * 64, 1024])),
    'out': tf.Variable(tf.random_normal([1024, n_classes]))
}

biases = {
    'b_conv1': tf.Variable(tf.random_normal([32])),
    'b_conv2': tf.Variable(tf.random_normal([64])),
    'b_fc': tf.Variable(tf.random_normal([1024])),
    'out': tf.Variable(tf.random_normal([n_classes]))
}

def conv2d(x, W):
    return tf.nn.conv2d(x, W, strides=[1, 1, 1, 1], padding='SAME')

def maxpool2d(x):
    return tf.nn.max_pool(x, ksize=[1, 2, 2, 1], strides=[1, 2, 2, 1], padding='SAME')

saver = tf.train.Saver()
sess = tf.Session()
saver.restore(sess, os.path.join(BASE_DIR, 'models/CNN/353epochs.txt'))

x = tf.placeholder('float', [None, 900])

def cnn_neural_network_model(x):
    x = tf.reshape(x, shape=[-1, 30, 30, 1])
    conv1 = tf.nn.relu(conv2d(x, weights['W_conv1']) + biases['b_conv1'])
    conv1 = maxpool2d(conv1)
    conv2 = tf.nn.relu(conv2d(conv1, weights['W_conv2']) + biases['b_conv2'])
    conv2 = maxpool2d(conv2)
    fc = tf.reshape(conv2, [-1, 8 * 8 * 64])
    fc = tf.nn.relu(tf.matmul(fc, weights['W_fc']) + biases['b_fc'])
    fc = tf.nn.dropout(fc, keep_rate)
    output = tf.matmul(fc, weights['out']) + biases['out']
    return output

def classify(image_data, is_image=False):
    if is_image:
        img = resize_data.resize_img(image_data, True)
    else:
        img = resize_data.resize_img(os.path.join(BASE_DIR + '/testing', image_data))
    x = np.array(img).flatten()
    prediction = cnn_neural_network_model([tf.cast(x, tf.float32)])
    result = sess.run(tf.argmax(tf.nn.softmax(prediction), 1))
    print(result)
    return result

if __name__ == "__main__":
    if len(sys.argv) == 1:
        print("No image path provided. Please provide an image path.")
    else:
        img_path = sys.argv[1]
        print('Classifying image:', img_path)
        classify(img_path)

# Test cases
# Assuming the resize_data and batch_maker modules are properly implemented and available in the environment
# Test case 1: Classify an image file
# classify('path/to/image.png', is_image=True)

# Test case 2: Classify an image represented as a NumPy array
# image_data = np.random.rand(30, 30)  # Example grayscale image data
# classify(image_data, is_image=True)
```

Note: The actual implementation of `resize_data` and `batch_maker` modules is not provided here, as they are assumed to be pre-existing modules in the user's environment. The test cases are commented out and should be run in an environment where these modules and the necessary model files are available.

Below is an end‐to‐end Python example that builds a CNN with two convolutional layers (each followed by ReLU and max‐pooling), one fully connected (dense) layer, and an output layer. The code shows how to initialize weights/biases, manually implement helper functions for 2D convolution and max‐pooling, load a pre‑trained model from file, preprocess images (using the assumed external module resize_data), and classify an image (or a batch) via a simple command‑line interface. (In this example the batch_maker module is used to create batches if needed.) You can adjust hyperparameters (number of filters, kernel sizes, etc.) and file names as required.

Below is the complete program:

------------------------------------------------
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
A CNN for image classification on 30x30 grayscale images that supports:
  • Building a CNN model with two convolutional layers, max‐pooling, a fully connected
    layer, and an output layer for n_classes classification.
  • Random initialization of weights and biases.
  • Manual implementations for 2D convolution and max-pooling helper functions.
  • Loading/restoring a pre-trained model (via tf.Session and tf.train.Saver).
  • Image preprocessing (resizing etc.) using an external module resize_data.
  • Classifying a single image or a batch of images.
  • A command‐line interface for user interaction.
Assumptions:
  – resize_data and batch_maker modules are available in the Python path.
  – The pre‐trained model is stored in a file (e.g., “./saved_model.ckpt”).
"""

import os
import argparse
import numpy as np
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow.python.framework import ops

# Assume these modules exist:
import resize_data  # provides resize() to resize an image to 30x30 if necessary
import batch_maker  # provides a function to create data batches, e.g., make_batch()

# For loading image files, we can use PIL
from PIL import Image


# ----- Helper functions for CNN operations -----
def conv2d(x, W, stride=1):
    """Apply 2D convolution."""
    return tf.nn.conv2d(x, W, strides=[1, stride, stride, 1], padding='SAME')


def max_pool(x, k=2):
    """Max pooling over 2x2 blocks."""
    return tf.nn.max_pool2d(x, ksize=[1, k, k, 1], strides=[1, k, k, 1], padding='SAME')


# ----- Build the CNN model -----
def build_cnn(x, n_classes):
    """Define the CNN architecture.
    Args:
      x: Input tensor of shape [batch_size, 30, 30, 1]
      n_classes: Number of output deep categories.
    Returns:
      The logits output of the network.
    """
    # First convolutional layer: 32 filters, 5x5 kernel, ReLU, then max pooling.
    conv1_W = tf.Variable(tf.random.truncated_normal([5, 5, 1, 32], stddev=0.1), name='conv1_W')
    conv1_b = tf.Variable(tf.constant(0.1, shape=[32]), name='conv1_b')
    conv1 = tf.nn.relu(conv2d(x, conv1_W) + conv1_b)
    pool1 = max_pool(conv1, k=2)

    # Second convolutional layer: 64 filters, 5x5 kernel, ReLU, then max pooling.
    conv2_W = tf.Variable(tf.random.truncated_normal([5, 5, 32, 64], stddev=0.1), name='conv2_W')
    conv2_b = tf.Variable(tf.constant(0.1, shape=[64]), name='conv2_b')
    conv2 = tf.nn.relu(conv2d(pool1, conv2_W) + conv2_b)
    pool2 = max_pool(conv2, k=2)

    # Flatten layer
    pool2_shape = pool2.get_shape().as_list()  # e.g., [batch_size, 8, 8, 64] for 30x30 input
    # Because the image size is small, dimensions might be smaller after pooling.
    flatten_dim = pool2_shape[1] * pool2_shape[2] * pool2_shape[3]
    flat = tf.reshape(pool2, [-1, flatten_dim])

    # Fully connected layer: 1024 neurons.
    fc_W = tf.Variable(tf.random.truncated_normal([flatten_dim, 1024], stddev=0.1), name='fc_W')
    fc_b = tf.Variable(tf.constant(0.1, shape=[1024]), name='fc_b')
    fc = tf.nn.relu(tf.matmul(flat, fc_W) + fc_b)

    # Output layer: logits no activation here.
    out_W = tf.Variable(tf.random.truncated_normal([1024, n_classes], stddev=0.1), name='out_W')
    out_b = tf.Variable(tf.constant(0.1, shape=[n_classes]), name='out_b')
    logits = tf.matmul(fc, out_W) + out_b

    return logits


# ----- Image Preprocessing -----
def load_and_preprocess_image(image_path):
    """
    Load an image file and preprocess:
      1. Open the image, convert it to grayscale.
      2. Resize it to 30x30 using the resize_data module.
      3. Normalize the pixel values.
    Returns a NumPy array of shape [30, 30, 1].
    """
    image = Image.open(image_path).convert('L')  # grayscale
    # Convert to numpy array
    image_np = np.array(image)
    # Use external module resize_data to resize if needed.
    image_resized = resize_data.resize(image_np, (30, 30))
    # Normalize (optional – here we scale pixels to [0,1])
    image_normalized = image_resized / 255.0
    # Reshape to [height, width, channels]
    image_final = np.reshape(image_normalized, (30, 30, 1))
    return image_final


def preprocess_np_image(image_np):
    """
    Preprocess an image already loaded as a NumPy array by:
      – Ensuring it’s grayscale.
      – Resizing it.
      – Normalizing.
    The function returns a NumPy array of shape [30, 30, 1].
    """
    # If it is not grayscale, convert it. (Assumes shape (H, W, C))
    if image_np.ndim == 3 and image_np.shape[2] != 1:
        # Convert to grayscale using average along channels.
        image_np = np.mean(image_np, axis=2)
    elif image_np.ndim == 2:
        # Already grayscale
        pass
    else:
        raise ValueError("Input image array has an unexpected number of dimensions.")
    # Resize using resize_data module.
    image_resized = resize_data.resize(image_np, (30, 30))
    image_normalized = image_resized / 255.0
    image_final = np.reshape(image_normalized, (30, 30, 1))
    return image_final


# ----- Classification function -----
def classify_images(image_batch, n_classes, sess, x_placeholder, logits, pred_op):
    """
    Classify a batch of images.
    Args:
       image_batch: numpy array of shape [batch_size, 30, 30, 1]
       n_classes: number of output classes.
       sess: a tf.Session() with the model restored.
       x_placeholder: the input placeholder.
       logits: the output logits tensor.
       pred_op: the predicted category indices.
    Returns:
       predictions: list of predicted indices.
    """
    feed_dict = {x_placeholder: image_batch}
    prediction = sess.run(pred_op, feed_dict=feed_dict)
    return prediction


# ----- Loading Pre-trained Model -----
def load_pretrained_model(sess, saver, model_path):
    """
    Loads the pretrained model from model_path using the given saver.
    """
    if os.path.exists(model_path + ".index"):
        saver.restore(sess, model_path)
        print("Model restored from:", model_path)
    else:
        print("No pre-trained model found at:", model_path)
        exit(1)


# ----- Main function with command-line interface -----
def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Classify images using a CNN.")
    parser.add_argument('--image', type=str, default=None,
                        help='Path to a single image file to classify.')
    parser.add_argument('--np_image', action='store_true',
                        help='Flag indicating that the input is a numpy array saved as a .npy file.')
    parser.add_argument('--batch', type=str, default=None,
                        help='Path to a .npy file containing a batch of images.')
    parser.add_argument('--model', type=str, default='./saved_model.ckpt',
                        help='Path to the pre-trained model checkpoint.')
    parser.add_argument('--n_classes', type=int, default=10,
                        help='Number of classes to classify.')
    args = parser.parse_args()

    # Create the graph
    tf.compat.v1.reset_default_graph()
    # Placeholder for input images: shape [batch_size, 30, 30, 1]
    x = tf.compat.v1.placeholder(tf.float32, shape=[None, 30, 30, 1], name='x')
    # Build the CNN model
    logits = build_cnn(x, args.n_classes)
    # For classification we pick the class with the highest logit
    pred = tf.argmax(logits, axis=1, output_type=tf.int32, name='pred')

    # Create a saver to restore the model later
    saver = tf.compat.v1.train.Saver()

    # Start session and load the pretrained model
    with tf.compat.v1.Session() as sess:
        sess.run(tf.compat.v1.global_variables_initializer())
        load_pretrained_model(sess, saver, args.model)

        # Prepare a batch of images to classify
        images_to_classify = []
        if args.image:
            # Classify a single image (or a numpy .npy if np_image flag is set)
            if args.np_image:
                # Load a numpy file assumed to have one image array.
                image_np = np.load(args.image)
                preprocessed = preprocess_np_image(image_np)
            else:
                preprocessed = load_and_preprocess_image(args.image)
            images_to_classify.append(preprocessed)
        elif args.batch:
            # Load a batch from .npy file (each image assumed to be in an array).
            # Let the batch maker module prepare the batch.
            batch = np.load(args.batch)  # assume shape: [batch_size, H, W] or [batch_size, H, W, C]
            # Process each image
            for img in batch:
                if img.ndim == 2 or (img.ndim == 3 and img.shape[-1] != 1):
                    img_proc = preprocess_np_image(img)
                else:
                    # Already in the correct shape?
                    img_proc = img
                images_to_classify.append(img_proc)
        else:
            print("Please specify either --image or --batch input.")
            exit(1)

        # Convert list to numpy array
        image_batch = np.array(images_to_classify)

        # Optionally use the batch_maker module to further process the batch.
        image_batch = batch_maker.make_batch(image_batch)

        # Run classification.
        predictions = classify_images(image_batch, args.n_classes, sess, x, logits, pred)
        print("Predicted class indices:")
        print(predictions)


if __name__ == '__main__':
    # Disable TF2 behavior for this legacy TF1-style code.
    tf.compat.v1.disable_eager_execution()
    main()

1. CNN Model Definition (build_cnn):
  • Two convolutional layers (with filters 32 and 64, kernel size 5×5) with ReLU activations.
  • Each conv layer is followed by a 2×2 max pooling operation (using our helper max_pool).
  • The output is flattened and passed to a fully-connected layer (1024 neurons), then an output layer producing logits for n_classes.

2. Helper Functions:
  • conv2d and max_pool functions serve as wrappers for tf.nn.conv2d and tf.nn.max_pool2d.

  • Using argparse, the user can supply an image file (--image) or a batch file (--batch) for classification. A flag (--np_image) allows processing of a numpy array file.

5. Batch Processing:
  • The external module batch_maker is used to prepare batches.

- `get_dbconn()`: Returns a database connection object.

```python
#! /usr/bin/env python
#-*- coding: utf-8 -*-

import modules_legacy.utils as utils

def clean_up_database():
    """
    Cleans up the database by removing records associated with inactive source IDs.
    Prints the SQL DELETE statements for records to be removed.
    """
    # Retrieve active source IDs
    active_sources = [int(x) for x in utils.get_sources().keys()]
    
    # Establish database connection
    dbconn = utils.get_dbconn()
    dbcurs = dbconn.cursor()
    
    # List of tables to clean up
    tables = ["markers_counts", "markers", "markers_status", "updates"]
    
    # Iterate over tables and clean up records with inactive source IDs
    for table in tables:
        dbcurs.execute(f"SELECT source_id FROM {table} GROUP BY source_id;")
        for record in dbcurs.fetchall():
            source_id = record[0]
            if source_id not in active_sources:
                print(f"DELETE FROM {table} WHERE source_id = {source_id};")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    clean_up_database()
```

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Database cleanup script for legacy systems.
This script removes records from specified tables whose source_id is no longer active.
It uses utility functions from modules_legacy.utils for obtaining active source IDs and connecting to the database.
"""

import sys
import logging
import unittest
from unittest import mock

# Import legacy utility functions (assumed to be provided)
from modules_legacy import utils

# Setup logging for audit purposes
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG, format='%(asctime)s %(levelname)s: %(message)s')

# Predefined list of table names that should be cleaned
TABLE_NAMES = ['table1', 'table2', 'table3']


def cleanup_database():
    """
    Connects to the database, retrieves active source IDs and cleans up records in predefined tables that have a source_id not active.
    """
    try:
        # Establish a database connection
        conn = utils.get_dbconn()
    except Exception as conn_err:
        logging.error("Failed to obtain database connection: %s", conn_err)
        sys.exit(1)

    try:
        # Get the dictionary of active sources, keys are active source IDs
        active_sources = utils.get_sources()
        active_source_ids = list(active_sources.keys())
        logging.info("Active source IDs: %s", active_source_ids)

        # Create a cursor from the connection
        cur = conn.cursor()

        for table in TABLE_NAMES:
            # If active_source_ids is not empty then only delete rows whose source_id is not active.
            # If active_source_ids is empty then delete all rows in the table.
            if active_source_ids:
                # Construct placeholders for parameterized query.
                placeholders = ', '.join(['%s'] * len(active_source_ids))
                sql = f"DELETE FROM {table} WHERE source_id NOT IN ({placeholders})"
                params = active_source_ids
            else:
                # When there are no active sources, this implies all records are inactive and should be removed.
                sql = f"DELETE FROM {table}"
                params = ()

            # Log the SQL that is about to be executed.
            logging.info("Executing SQL: %s with params: %s", sql, params)
            print("SQL to execute:", sql, " | params:", params)

            try:
                cur.execute(sql, params)
                # Some DB APIs (like psycopg2) let you access cursor.rowcount after an execute.
                deleted_count = cur.rowcount
                logging.info("Deleted %s records from table %s", deleted_count, table)
            except Exception as exec_err:
                logging.error("Error executing SQL on table %s: %s", table, exec_err)
                conn.rollback()
                continue

        # Commit the changes after processing all tables
        conn.commit()
    except Exception as err:
        logging.error("An error occurred during cleanup: %s", err)
        conn.rollback()
    finally:
        try:
            cur.close()
            conn.close()
        except Exception:
            pass


# Unit tests for the cleanup_database function.
class TestCleanupDatabase(unittest.TestCase):

    def setUp(self):
        # Patch the utils.get_dbconn and utils.get_sources functions.
        self.get_dbconn_patcher = mock.patch('modules_legacy.utils.get_dbconn')
        self.get_sources_patcher = mock.patch('modules_legacy.utils.get_sources')

        self.mock_get_dbconn = self.get_dbconn_patcher.start()
        self.mock_get_sources = self.get_sources_patcher.start()

        # Create a fake connection and cursor.
        self.fake_cursor = mock.MagicMock()
        self.fake_conn = mock.MagicMock()
        self.fake_conn.cursor.return_value = self.fake_cursor
        self.mock_get_dbconn.return_value = self.fake_conn

    def tearDown(self):
        self.get_dbconn_patcher.stop()
        self.get_sources_patcher.stop()

    def test_cleanup_with_active_sources(self):
        # Simulate active sources with two source IDs.
        active_sources = {'src1': 'info1', 'src2': 'info2'}
        self.mock_get_sources.return_value = active_sources

        # Make rowcount return a fake deletion count.
        self.fake_cursor.rowcount = 5

        # Call the cleanup function.
        cleanup_database()

        # There should be one call per table for execute
        self.assertEqual(self.fake_cursor.execute.call_count, len(TABLE_NAMES))

        # Check one of the calls: It should include the proper SQL with placeholders.
        placeholders = ', '.join(['%s'] * len(active_sources))
        expected_sql = f"DELETE FROM {TABLE_NAMES[0]} WHERE source_id NOT IN ({placeholders})"
        self.fake_cursor.execute.assert_any_call(expected_sql, list(active_sources.keys()))

        # Ensure that commit was called.
        self.fake_conn.commit.assert_called_once()

    def test_cleanup_with_empty_active_sources(self):
        # Simulate an empty list of active sources.
        self.mock_get_sources.return_value = {}

        # Make rowcount return a fake deletion count.
        self.fake_cursor.rowcount = 10

        # Call the cleanup function.
        cleanup_database()

        # There should be one call per table for execute with a SQL query without WHERE clause.
        self.assertEqual(self.fake_cursor.execute.call_count, len(TABLE_NAMES))
        for table in TABLE_NAMES:
            expected_sql = f"DELETE FROM {table}"
            self.fake_cursor.execute.assert_any_call(expected_sql, ())

        # Ensure that commit was called.
        self.fake_conn.commit.assert_called_once()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    # If tests are requested (e.g., via command line argument "test"), run the tests,
    # otherwise run the cleanup_database.
    if len(sys.argv) > 1 and sys.argv[1] == "test":
        # Remove the "test" argument before running unittest.main()
        sys.argv.pop(1)
        unittest.main()
    else:
        cleanup_database()

2. For each table in TABLE_NAMES, if active IDs exist, a DELETE statement is prepared using parameter placeholders; if not, a simple DELETE is executed (which removes all rows for that table).

The program should also handle large input validation and provide appropriate feedback.

The Caesar cipher is a type of substitution cipher in which each letter in the plaintext is shifted a certain number of places down or up the alphabet. For example, with a shift of 1, 'A' would be replaced by 'B', 'B' would become 'C', and so on.

Binary encoding represents text as a sequence of binary numbers, where each character is converted to its corresponding binary ASCII value.

The program should include the following functionalities:
1. Encrypt a given text using the Caesar cipher with a specified shift.
2. Decrypt a given binary-encoded string back to text.
3. Validate that the input text for encryption does not exceed a certain length (e.g., 4096 characters).
4. Provide appropriate feedback for invalid inputs or errors.

```python
def caesar_cipher_encrypt(text, shift):
    """
    Encrypts the given text using a Caesar cipher with the specified shift.
    
    :param text: The text to be encrypted.
    :param shift: The number of positions to shift each character.
    :return: The encrypted text.
    """
    encrypted_text = ""
    for char in text:
        if char.isalpha():
            shifted = ord(char) + shift
            if char.islower():
                if shifted > ord('z'):
                    shifted -= 26
                elif shifted < ord('a'):
                    shifted += 26
            elif char.isupper():
                if shifted > ord('Z'):
                    shifted -= 26
                elif shifted < ord('A'):
                    shifted += 26
            encrypted_text += chr(shifted)
        else:
            encrypted_text += char
    return encrypted_text

def binary_to_text(binary_string):
    """
    Converts a binary-encoded string back to text.
    
    :param binary_string: The binary string to be converted.
    :return: The decoded text.
    """
    binary_values = binary_string.split()
    text = "".join([chr(int(b, 2)) for b in binary_values])
    return text

def validate_input(text, max_length=4096):
    """
    Validates that the input text does not exceed the maximum length.
    
    :param text: The text to be validated.
    :param max_length: The maximum allowed length of the text.
    :return: A tuple (is_valid, message).
    """
    if len(text) > max_length:
        return False, f"Error: The input text exceeds the maximum allowed length of {max_length} characters."
    return True, "Input text is valid."

# Test cases
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Test encryption
    original_text = "Hello, World!"
    shift = 3
    encrypted = caesar_cipher_encrypt(original_text, shift)
    print(f"Encrypted text: {encrypted}")

    # Test decryption
    binary_string = "01001000 01100101 01101100 01101100 01101111"
    decrypted = binary_to_text(binary_string)
    print(f"Decrypted text: {decrypted}")

    # Test input validation
    long_text = "a" * 5000
    is_valid, message = validate_input(long_text)
    print(message)
```

Below is one complete solution in Python. The program defines two main functions—one that encrypts plain alphabetic text using a Caesar cipher (and then converts the encrypted text into an 8‐bit binary representation for each character) and another that “decrypts” (i.e. decodes) a given binary string back into text. In addition, the program validates that the input text for encryption is no longer than 4096 characters and contains only alphabetic characters. Furthermore, unit tests for both functions are included so you can verify correctness.

Below is the full source code:

------------------------------------------------------------
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Text Encryption/Decryption Service

This program supports:
1. Encrypting a given text using a Caesar cipher with a specified shift.
   It first validates that the text is within 4096 characters in length and contains only alphabetic characters.
   The encryption shifts each letter by the given integer (wrapping around the alphabet), 
   and then converts each encrypted character to its 8-bit binary ASCII representation.
2. Decrypting a binary-encoded string back to text.
   The function expects a whitespace-delimited sequence of binary strings (each representing an 8-bit ASCII value)
   and converts them into the corresponding characters.
   
Usage:
  - Run the script and follow the prompts, or import the functions into other modules.
  
Unit tests are defined in the TestCipherFunctions class.
"""

def caesar_encrypt(text, shift):
    """
    Encrypts the given text using a Caesar cipher and then returns the binary encoding of the encrypted text.
    
    Parameters:
      text (str): Plain text to encrypt. Must be no more than 4096 characters and contain only alphabetic characters.
      shift (int): The integer shift to apply.
    
    Returns:
      str: A single string composed of 8-bit binary numbers for each encrypted character, separated by spaces.
      
    Raises:
      ValueError: If the text exceeds 4096 characters or if any non-alphabetic characters are present.
    """
    # Validate maximum length
    if len(text) > 4096:
        raise ValueError("Input text exceeds maximum allowed length (4096 characters).")
    
    # Validate that every character is alphabetic (no spaces, punctuation, etc.)
    if not all(char.isalpha() for char in text):
        raise ValueError("Encryption input contains non-alphabetic characters.")
    
    encrypted_chars = []
    for char in text:
        # Check if the char is uppercase or lowercase and compute the shifted value
        if char.isupper():
            # 'A' == 65 in ASCII
            new_char = chr((ord(char) - ord('A') + shift) % 26 + ord('A'))
        else:
            # lowercase
            new_char = chr((ord(char) - ord('a') + shift) % 26 + ord('a'))
        encrypted_chars.append(new_char)
    
    encrypted_text = ''.join(encrypted_chars)
    
    # Convert each character of the encrypted text to an 8-bit binary string.
    binary_encoded = ' '.join(format(ord(c), '08b') for c in encrypted_text)
    return binary_encoded


def binary_to_text(binary_str):
    """
    Decrypts a binary-encoded string back to text.
    
    The binary string should consist of space-separated 8-bit binary numbers.
    Handles leading zeros in each binary number.
    
    Parameters:
      binary_str (str): Binary string input.
      
    Returns:
      str: The decoded text.
      
    Raises:
      ValueError: If a token in binary_str contains characters other than '0' or '1' or if conversion fails.
    """
    tokens = binary_str.split()
    characters = []
    for token in tokens:
        if not all(ch in "01" for ch in token):
            raise ValueError(f"Binary token '{token}' contains invalid characters.")
        try:
            number = int(token, 2)
            characters.append(chr(number))
        except Exception as e:
            raise ValueError(f"Invalid binary token '{token}': {str(e)}")
    return ''.join(characters)


def main():
    """
    Main function: Provides a simple text-based interface for encryption and decryption.
    """
    print("Welcome to the Text Encryption/Decryption Service!")
    print("Choose an option:")
    print("1. Encrypt text using a Caesar cipher")
    print("2. Decrypt a binary-encoded string back to text")
    
    choice = input("Enter 1 or 2: ")
    
    if choice == "1":
        text = input("Enter the text to encrypt (alphabetic characters only, no spaces/punctuation): ")
        shift_input = input("Enter the shift as an integer: ")
        try:
            shift = int(shift_input)
        except ValueError:
            print("Invalid shift value. Please enter an integer.")
            return
        
        try:
            encrypted_binary = caesar_encrypt(text, shift)
            print(f"Encrypted (binary encoded) text:\n{encrypted_binary}")
        except ValueError as err:
            print("Encryption error:", err)
    
    elif choice == "2":
        binary_str = input("Enter the binary-encoded string (space separated 8-bit values): ")
        try:
            decrypted_text = binary_to_text(binary_str)
            print("Decrypted text:")
            print(decrypted_text)
        except ValueError as err:
            print("Decryption error:", err)
    else:
        print("Invalid choice. Exiting.")


# Unit tests for the functions
if __name__ == '__main__':
    # Uncomment the following line to run the main interface:
    # main()
    
    # When executing this script directly, run the unit tests.
    import unittest

    class TestCipherFunctions(unittest.TestCase):
        def test_caesar_encrypt_basic(self):
            # Simple case: shift by 1
            result = caesar_encrypt("abc", 1)
            # Encrypted text should be 'bcd' -> binary codes for b, c, d.
            expected = '01100010 01100011 01100100'
            self.assertEqual(result, expected)
        
        def test_caesar_encrypt_wraparound(self):
            # Test wraparound for uppercase and lowercase
            result = caesar_encrypt("Zz", 1)
            expected = '01000001 01100001'   # 'A' and 'a'
            self.assertEqual(result, expected)
        
        def test_caesar_encrypt_invalid_characters(self):
            # Text contains invalid character (space or punctuation)
            with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
                caesar_encrypt("Hello World", 3)
        
        def test_caesar_encrypt_too_long(self):
            # Create a text with length > 4096
            text = "a" * 4097
            with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
                caesar_encrypt(text, 3)
        
        def test_binary_to_text_basic(self):
            # Test a basic binary to text conversion
            binary_input = "01101000 01101001"  # 'h' and 'i'
            result = binary_to_text(binary_input)
            self.assertEqual(result, "hi")
        
        def test_binary_to_text_leading_zeros(self):
            # Test tokens with leading zeros
            binary_input = "00001000"
            result = binary_to_text(binary_input)
            self.assertEqual(result, "\x08")  # ASCII backspace or control char
        
        def test_binary_to_text_invalid_token(self):
            # Token that contains invalid characters
            with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
                binary_to_text("0110a010")
    
    # Run the tests if this script is executed
    unittest.main(verbosity=2, exit=False)

Each character is then shifted by the given value with wrap‐around (using modulo 26), preserving case. Finally, the encrypted text is converted into 8-bit binary strings (using format(ord(c), '08b')) for each character.

2. The function binary_to_text(binary_str) splits the input by whitespace (so tokens like "01101000") and verifies that each token is a binary string. It converts these tokens from base‑2 integer form into their corresponding ASCII characters.

3. A simple text interface is provided in the main() function. You can uncomment the main() call in the __main__ block to enable the interactive console.

Below is one possible implementation in Python. In this design we use the spaCy library for part‐of‐speech tagging (to find both common and proper nouns), the dateutil.parser from the python‑dateutil library to “fuzzily” detect a date in the sentence, and a helper function to convert numbers in digit‐form or a few spelled‐out numbers into integers. (In production you might want to use a more comprehensive number‐word conversion library.) We also allow an optional dictionary of word classes (mapping a class name to a list of words) and a flag skip_first that tells the utility to ignore the first token when matching for word classes. Finally, several unit tests (via Python’s unittest module) exercise edge cases.

To try the code, make sure you have installed the dependencies:
  pip install spacy python-dateutil
and download spaCy’s English model:
  python -m spacy download en_core_web_sm

Below is the complete code:

------------------------------------------------
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import re
import unittest
from datetime import datetime
from dateutil.parser import parse as date_parse, ParserError

import spacy

# Load spaCy’s English model
nlp = spacy.load("en_core_web_sm")


# A helper to convert a token that contains a number. We try to convert digit strings directly.
# For some simple number words, we include a basic mapping.
NUMBER_WORDS = {
    "zero": 0, "one": 1, "two": 2, "three": 3, "four": 4, "five": 5,
    "six": 6, "seven": 7, "eight": 8, "nine": 9, "ten": 10, "eleven": 11, "twelve": 12,
    "thirteen": 13, "fourteen": 14, "fifteen": 15, "sixteen": 16, "seventeen": 17,
    "eighteen": 18, "nineteen": 19, "twenty": 20
}

def convert_to_int(text):
    # Remove commas from numbers like "1,234"
    text = text.replace(",", "")
    try:
        return int(text)
    except ValueError:
        # Try to match simple number words (case-insensitive)
        low = text.lower()
        if low in NUMBER_WORDS:
            return NUMBER_WORDS[low]
        # Attempt to extract digits embedded in the string
        m = re.search(r'\d+', text)
        if m:
            return int(m.group(0))
    return None


def nlp_analyze(sentence, word_classes=None, skip_first=False):
    """
    Analyzes the input sentence and extracts:
      - lastnoun: the last noun (or proper noun) found in the sentence.
      - nouns: a list of all nouns found in the sentence.
      - numbers: a list of all numbers found in the sentence, converted to integers.
      - date: a date found in the sentence (if any) formatted as "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS".
      - word_classes: a list of class names (from the provided word_classes dictionary)
                      found in the sentence.
    Parameters:
      sentence (str): The sentence to analyze.
      word_classes (dict): Optional dictionary mapping a class name to a list of words.
                           Example: {"vehicles": ["car","bus"], "icecreamflavours": ["vanilla", "chocolate"] }
      skip_first (bool): If True, skip the first word when matching for word classes.
    Returns:
      dict: A dictionary containing the keys 'lastnoun', 'nouns', 'numbers', 'date', and 'word_classes'.
    """
    result = {
        "lastnoun": None,
        "nouns": [],
        "numbers": [],
        "date": None,
        "word_classes": []
    }
    
    # If input is empty, return empty/default values.
    if not sentence or not sentence.strip():
        return result

    doc = nlp(sentence)

    # Process tokens for nouns and numbers.
    last_noun = None
    for token in doc:
        # Using simple spaCy POS tags: 'NOUN' for common and 'PROPN' for proper nouns.
        if token.pos_ in ['NOUN', 'PROPN']:
            result["nouns"].append(token.text)
            last_noun = token.text
        
        # Identify numbers using token.like_num. Then attempt conversion.
        if token.like_num:
            num = convert_to_int(token.text)
            if num is not None:
                result["numbers"].append(num)

    result["lastnoun"] = last_noun

    # Look for date in the sentence using dateutil.parser.parse with fuzzy=True.
    try:
        # The fuzzy_with_tokens option returns a tuple (datetime, list_of_unused_tokens)
        dt, _ = date_parse(sentence, fuzzy_with_tokens=True)
        # Format the date in "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS" format.
        result["date"] = dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
    except (ParserError, ValueError):
        # No date found – leave as None.
        result["date"] = None

    # Process word classes if provided.
    if word_classes and isinstance(word_classes, dict):
        # Optionally skip a token: we decide which tokens to consider 
        tokens_to_check = list(doc)[1:] if skip_first else doc
        matched_classes = set()
        # Lowercase the tokens for matching.
        tokens_text = {token.text.lower() for token in tokens_to_check}
        # For each word class, check if any of its words (lowercased) appear in the sentence.
        for cls, words in word_classes.items():
            for word in words:
                if word.lower() in tokens_text:
                    matched_classes.add(cls)
                    break
        result["word_classes"] = list(matched_classes)
    else:
        result["word_classes"] = []

    return result


# ---------------- Unit Tests -----------------
class TestNLPAnalyze(unittest.TestCase):

    def test_empty_sentence(self):
        self.assertEqual(nlp_analyze(""),
                         {"lastnoun": None, "nouns": [], "numbers": [], "date": None, "word_classes": []})
    
    def test_sentence_with_nouns_numbers_date(self):
        sentence = "John bought 2 apples on 2023-09-15 at the market."
        # Expected: lastnoun may be "market" (if spaCy tags it as noun); nouns include "John", "apples", "market"
        result = nlp_analyze(sentence)
        self.assertIn("John", result["nouns"])
        self.assertIn("apples", result["nouns"])
        self.assertIn("market", result["nouns"])
        self.assertEqual(result["numbers"], [2])
        # Check date formatting contains expected year-month day etc.
        self.assertIsNotNone(result["date"])
        try:
            datetime.strptime(result["date"], "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
        except ValueError:
            self.fail("Date format incorrect!")
    
    def test_sentence_with_word_numbers(self):
        # A sentence with a number in word form.
        sentence = "Alice sees three cats and one dog."
        result = nlp_analyze(sentence)
        # With our basic mapping, "three" and "one" are in our mapping.
        self.assertEqual(sorted(result["numbers"]), sorted([3, 1]))
    
    def test_sentence_with_mixed_date_formats(self):
        # The date in this sentence is in a more natural format.
        sentence = "The event is scheduled for July 4, 2022 at 9:00 AM."
        result = nlp_analyze(sentence)
        # Ensure date is detected and formatted.
        self.assertIsNotNone(result["date"])
        try:
            dt = datetime.strptime(result["date"], "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
        except ValueError:
            self.fail("Date format incorrect!")
    
    def test_sentence_with_word_classes(self):
        sentence = "I drove my car near a bank while eating vanilla ice cream."
        word_classes = {"vehicles": ["car", "truck", "bus"], "icecreamflavours": ["vanilla", "chocolate"]}
        # Without skipping, both classes are matched.
        result = nlp_analyze(sentence, word_classes=word_classes, skip_first=False)
        self.assertCountEqual(result["word_classes"], ["vehicles", "icecreamflavours"])
    
    def test_skip_first_word(self):
        # When skip_first is True, if the first word belongs to a word class it should not count.
        sentence = "Car owners love to drive fast."
        word_classes = {"vehicles": ["car"], "speed": ["fast"]}
        # Since skip_first=True, "Car" is skipped for matching word classes.
        result = nlp_analyze(sentence, word_classes=word_classes, skip_first=True)
        # Only "fast" should match => "speed"
        self.assertEqual(result["word_classes"], ["speed"])

    def test_no_nouns(self):
        # A sentence that does not contain any noun.
        sentence = "Quickly and silently, they ran."
        result = nlp_analyze(sentence)
        self.assertEqual(result["nouns"], [])
        self.assertIsNone(result["lastnoun"])


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Run unit tests.
    unittest.main()

------------------------------------------------

Explanation of key parts:

1. The function first checks if the sentence is empty.  
2. spaCy is used to iterate over tokens to capture nouns (both common and proper) and numbers (using the token’s like_num flag).
3. A helper function convert_to_int converts digit strings or simple spelled-out numbers (using a basic dictionary) into integers.
4. The dateutil.parser.parse function with fuzzy matching tries to extract a date from the sentence. If found, it is formatted as a string “YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS”.
5. The optional word_classes parameter (a dictionary) is used to check which classes’ words are present in the sentence – optionally ignoring the first token if skip_first is True.
6. Several unit tests cover edge cases including mixed date/number formats, skipping tokens in word classes, and sentences without nouns.

This design meets the requirements and demonstrates how to handle different sentence structures for the extraction of nouns, numbers, dates, and predefined word classes.

Create a Python Django application that allows users to search for wallpapers from the Wallhaven website (https://wallhaven.cc/). The application should provide a form where users can enter a search phrase to find wallpapers related to that phrase or choose to get random wallpapers. The search results should be displayed as thumbnails on the same page without reloading the entire page (using AJAX). Each thumbnail should be encoded in base64 to be displayed directly in the HTML.

The application should consist of the following components:
1. A Django form (`WallpaperForm`) with fields for the search phrase and a boolean field to indicate whether the user wants random wallpapers.
2. A view function (`wallpaper`) that handles the form submission and returns a JSON response with the base64-encoded images if the request is made via AJAX, or renders the form on the page if it's a regular GET request.
3. A helper function (`convert_images`) that takes the search phrase and a boolean indicating random or not, fetches the images from Wallhaven, and returns a list of tuples with the image extension and base64-encoded data.
4. A template (`home.html`) that includes the form and a script to handle the AJAX submission and update the page with the search results.
5. A template (`search_results.html`) to render the base64-encoded images as thumbnails.
code:
```python
# Required imports
import base64
import re
from concurrent import futures
import requests
from django.http import JsonResponse
from django.shortcuts import render
from django.template.loader import render_to_string
from .forms import WallpaperForm

# View function to handle wallpaper search and AJAX requests
def wallpaper(request):
    form = WallpaperForm(data=request.POST or None)
    if request.method == 'POST' and form.is_valid() and request.is_ajax():
        template = convert_images(form.cleaned_data.get('search_phrase'), form.cleaned_data.get('random'))
        return JsonResponse({'template': template})
    return render(request, 'wallpaper/home.html', {'form': form})

# Helper function to fetch and convert images to base64
def convert_images(search_phrase, random=None):
    if random:
        response = requests.get('https://alpha.wallhaven.cc/random?page=2').text
    else:
        response = requests.get('https://alpha.wallhaven.cc/search?q={0}&purity=100&resolutions=1920x1080&sorting=relevance&order=desc&page=1'.format(search_phrase)).text

    data = re.findall('data-src="https://alpha.wallhaven.cc/wallpapers/thumb/small/th-(.+?)" src=', response)

    with futures.ThreadPoolExecutor(len(data)) as executor:
        # create generator
        result = executor.map(make_base64_image, data)

    result = filter(bool, result)
    return render_to_string('wallpaper/search_results.html', context={'result': result})

# Helper function to make a single base64-encoded image
def make_base64_image(index):
    extensions = {'png', 'jpg'}
    index, extension = index.split('.')
    response = requests.get('https://wallpapers.wallhaven.cc/wallpapers/full/wallhaven-{}.{}'.format(index, extension))

    # Handle different extensions for thumbnails and full images
    if response.status_code != 200:
        extension = extensions.difference(set(extension)).pop()
        response = requests.get('https://wallpapers.wallhaven.cc/wallpapers/full/wallhaven-{}.{}'.format(index, extension))
        if response.status_code != 200:
            return None

    content = response.content
    data = base64.b64encode(content)
    data = data.decode('ascii')
    return extension, data

# 'home.html' template should include the form and AJAX script
# 'search_results.html' template should render the base64-encoded images as thumbnails
```

4. `protos`: A list of strings representing the protobuf files.

code:
```python
import textwrap

def generate_rust_protobuf_library(name, srcs, build_script, protos, build_env=None, deps=None):
    """
    Generates a string that represents a configuration for a Rust library with protobuf support.

    :param name: The name of the Rust library.
    :param srcs: The source files for the Rust library.
    :param build_script: The path to the build script.
    :param protos: The protobuf files.
    :param build_env: The build environment variables (optional).
    :param deps: The dependencies for the Rust library (optional).
    :return: A string representing the configuration.
    """
    build_name = name + "-build"
    proto_name = name + "-proto"
    build_env = build_env or {}
    build_env.update({
        "PROTOC": "$(exe fbsource//third-party/protobuf:protoc)",
        "PROTOC_INCLUDE": "$(location fbsource//third-party/protobuf:google.protobuf)",
    })
    deps = deps or []

    config = textwrap.dedent(f"""\
        buck_rust_binary(
            name = "{build_name}",
            srcs = ["{build_script}"],
            crate_root = "{build_script}",
            deps = [
                "//buck2/app/buck2_protoc_dev:buck2_protoc_dev",
            ],
        )

        buck_genrule(
            name = "{proto_name}",
            srcs = {protos},
            cmd = "$(exe :{build_name}) --required-for-buck1=$OUT",
            env = {build_env},
            out = ".",
        )

        rust_library(
            name = "{name}",
            srcs = {srcs},
            env = {{
                "OUT_DIR": "$(location :{proto_name})",
            }},
            deps = [
                "fbsource//third-party/rust:prost",
                "fbsource//third-party/rust:tonic",
            ] + {deps},
        )

        # For python tests only
        {export_files}
    """)
    
    export_files = "\n".join([f'export_file(name = "{proto}",)' for proto in protos])
    return config.format(export_files=export_files)

# Test cases
print(generate_rust_protobuf_library(
    name="my_rust_lib",
    srcs=["src/lib.rs"],
    build_script="build.rs",
    protos=["proto1.proto", "proto2.proto"],
    build_env={"CUSTOM_VAR": "value"},
    deps=["//some/dependency:dep"]
))
```

def generate_rust_protobuf_library(name, srcs, build_script, protos, build_env=None, deps=None):
    """
    Generates a configuration string for a Rust library with protobuf support.
    
    Parameters:
      name (str): Name of the Rust library.
      srcs (list of str): List of Rust source file paths.
      build_script (str): Path to the build script.
      protos (list of str): List of protobuf file paths.
      build_env (dict, optional): Dictionary of build environment variables.
      deps (list of str, optional): List of dependency names.
    
    Returns:
      str: A configuration string that includes buck_rust_binary, buck_genrule,
           rust_library, and export_file configurations.
    """
    
    # Format lists as Buck-style string literals.
    fmt_list = lambda lst: ", ".join(f'"{item}"' for item in lst)
    srcs_str = fmt_list(srcs)
    protos_str = fmt_list(protos)
    
    # Use empty list if deps is None.
    deps = deps or []
    deps_str = fmt_list(deps)
    
    # If build_env is provided, format it as Buck dictionary entries.
    env_str = ""
    if build_env:
        env_entries = ", ".join(f'"{key}": "{value}"' for key, value in build_env.items())
        env_str = f"    env = {{{env_entries}}},\n"
    
    # Generate a configuration string with four parts.
    # 1. buck_rust_binary: builds a Rust binary that may be used by the protobuf generator.
    rust_binary = (
f'buck_rust_binary(\n'
f'    name = "{name}_bin",\n'
f'    srcs = [{srcs_str}],\n'
f'    deps = [{deps_str}],\n'
f')\n'
    )
    
    # 2. buck_genrule: generates Rust code from protobufs.
    # The command assumes "protoc" is available, using the binary target location.
    gen_rule = (
f'\nbuck_genrule(\n'
f'    name = "{name}_genproto",\n'
f'    srcs = [{protos_str}],\n'
f'    out = "{name}_proto.rs",\n'
f'    cmd = "protoc --rust_out=$(location {name}_bin) $(SRCS)",\n'
f'{env_str}'
f'    deps = [":{name}_bin"],\n'
f')\n'
    )
    
    # 3. rust_library: the actual Rust library that includes the source files and generated code.
    # If there are additional deps provided, they are appended.
    rust_library = (
f'\nrust_library(\n'
f'    name = "{name}",\n'
f'    srcs = [{srcs_str}, "{name}_proto.rs"],\n'
f'    deps = [":{name}_bin"{", " + deps_str if deps_str else ""}],\n'
f')\n'
    )
    
    # 4. export_file: exports the build script file.
    export = (
f'\nexport_file(\n'
f'    name = "{name}_build_script",\n'
f'    src = "{build_script}",\n'
f')\n'
    )
    
    # Combine all parts together.
    configuration = rust_binary + gen_rule + rust_library + export
    return configuration

# Example usage:
if __name__ == "__main__":
    config_str = generate_rust_protobuf_library(
        name="my_rust_lib",
        srcs=["src/lib.rs", "src/utils.rs"],
        build_script="build/build.rs",
        protos=["proto/service.proto", "proto/messages.proto"],
        build_env={"PROTOC_VERSION": "3.17.3", "TARGET": "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"},
        deps=["//third_party:some_dep"]
    )
    print(config_str)

The class should provide methods to check if a token exists, add a new session, and remove an existing session. The `SessionsDAO` class should inherit from a generic `DAO` class that handles common database operations. The `SessionsDAO` class should use PostgreSQL as the underlying database, and it should handle timezones correctly when storing session creation times.

The `SessionsDAO` class should implement the following methods:

- `__init__(self)`: Initializes the `SessionsDAO` instance, setting the table name to 'sessions' and a secret key for internal use.
- `isTokenExist(self, token)`: Checks if a session with the given token exists in the database.
- `add(self, user_id, duration, token)`: Adds a new session for a user with the given `user_id`, `duration` (in seconds), and `token`. If a session for the user already exists, it should update the existing session with the new `created_at` timestamp and `token`. The `created_at` timestamp should be stored in UTC.
- `remove(self, token)`: Removes the session with the given token from the database.

The `DAO` class is not provided, but you can assume it has a method `__perform_db_req__(self, query, params)` that executes a given SQL `query` with `params` against the database and returns the result.

```python
import psycopg2
from datetime import datetime, timezone

class DAO:
    def __init__(self, table):
        self.table = table
        self.conn = psycopg2.connect("dbname=test user=postgres password=secret")

    def __perform_db_req__(self, query, params):
        with self.conn.cursor() as cur:
            cur.execute(query, params)
            self.conn.commit()
            return cur.rowcount

class SessionsDAO(DAO):
    def __init__(self):
        self.table = 'sessions'
        self.SECRET = 'secret...'
        super(SessionsDAO, self).__init__(self.table)
    
    def isTokenExist(self, token):
        query = 'select exists(select 1 from sessions where token = %s)'
        return self.__perform_db_req__(query, (token,))
    
    def add(self, user_id, duration, token):
        created_at = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
        query = ('insert into sessions (user_id, created_at, duration, token) '
                 'values (%s, %s::timestamp, %s, %s) '
                 'on conflict (user_id) do update '
                 'set '
                 '(created_at, token) = (EXCLUDED.created_at, EXCLUDED.token)')
        return self.__perform_db_req__(query, (user_id, created_at, duration, token))
    
    def remove(self, token):
        query = 'delete from sessions where token = %s'
        return self.__perform_db_req__(query, (token,))

# Test cases to verify the solution correctness
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Assuming the database and table are already set up
    dao = SessionsDAO()
    
    # Test adding a session
    user_id = 1
    duration = 3600  # 1 hour in seconds
    token = 'abc123'
    add_result = dao.add(user_id, duration, token)
    print(f"Add session result: {add_result}")  # Should print the number of rows affected
    
    # Test checking if a token exists
    token_exist = dao.isTokenExist(token)
    print(f"Token exists: {token_exist}")  # Should print True if the token exists
    
    # Test removing a session
    remove_result = dao.remove(token)
    print(f"Remove session result: {remove_result}")  # Should print the number of rows affected
```

Note: The actual implementation of the `DAO` class and the database setup are not provided. The test cases assume that the database and the `sessions` table are already set up with the appropriate schema. The `psycopg2` library is used for PostgreSQL database interactions.

In this example the base DAO is “faked” with an in‐memory list that simulates the PostgreSQL table “sessions.” (In a production system the DAO would connect to PostgreSQL and use parameterized queries to avoid SQL injection attacks.) Notice that all queries use parameter placeholders (e.g. %s) so that the underlying database adapter can safely substitute values without risking SQL injection. Also, the created_at timestamps are generated in UTC using Python’s timezone‐aware datetime objects.

Below is the full code:
